message.content:
Let the wall temperature excess be

\[
T_w-T_\infty=\frac{C}{x},
\]

with \(C\) a constant, and let \(x\) be measured along the vertical surface from the leading edge. Let \(u\) be the velocity component along the surface and \(v\) the normal component.

The local buoyancy acceleration is

\[
g\beta(T_w-T_\infty)=\frac{g\beta C}{x}.
\]

For a laminar natural-convection boundary layer, balance the dominant scales:

\[
\frac{u_{\max}^2}{x}\sim \frac{g\beta C}{x},
\qquad
\frac{\nu u_{\max}}{\delta^2}\sim \frac{g\beta C}{x},
\]

and for the temperature field,

\[
\frac{u_{\max}(T_w-T_\infty)}{x}
\sim
\frac{\alpha(T_w-T_\infty)}{\delta^2}.
\]

With \(T_w-T_\infty\propto x^{-1}\), these give

\[
u_{\max}\sim (g\beta C)^{1/2}=O(1),
\]

and

\[
\delta^2\sim \frac{\nu u_{\max}}{g\beta C/x}\propto x,
\qquad
\delta\propto x^{1/2}.
\]

The energy balance checks the same \(x\)-dependence; the numerical constants may depend on \(Pr\).

Then:

\[
q''=k\left|\frac{\partial T}{\partial y}\right|_w
\sim k\frac{T_w-T_\infty}{\delta}
\sim kC\,x^{-1}\,x^{-1/2}
\propto x^{-3/2}.
\]

If \(Q\) is the total heat rate per unit spanwise width associated with a length \(x\),

\[
Q\sim \int q''\,dx \sim \int x^{-3/2}\,dx,
\]

so, up to an additive constant set by any finite leading-edge regularization,

\[
Q\propto x^{-1/2}.
\]

Equivalently, in the simple local-order sense, \(Q\sim q''x\propto x^{-1/2}\). The ideal integral from \(x=0\) diverges because the prescribed wall temperature is singular at the leading edge.

From continuity,

\[
v(\infty)\sim -\frac{d}{dx}\int_0^\infty u\,dy
\sim -\frac{d(u_{\max}\delta)}{dx},
\]

so with \(u_{\max}=O(1)\) and \(\delta\propto x^{1/2}\),

\[
v(\infty)\propto x^{-1/2}
\]

in magnitude; the sign depends on the chosen coordinate direction and whether the wall is heated or cooled.

Thus the required variations are

\[
\boxed{
q''\propto x^{-3/2},\qquad
Q\propto x^{-1/2},\qquad
\delta\propto x^{1/2},\qquad
u_{\max}\propto x^0,\qquad
v(\infty)\propto x^{-1/2}
}
\]

for the magnitudes in the usual laminar natural-convection boundary-layer regime.

This exact \(1/x\) condition is not physically realizable all the way down to \(x=0\), because \(T_w\), \(q''\), and \(v(\infty)\) become singular and the ideal integrated heat rate from zero is infinite. It is, however, physically meaningful as a far-field or asymptotic condition if the leading-edge singularity is regularized by a finite-size heater. For example, a vertical surface heated by a small localized point or narrow heat source at its leading edge in a constant-temperature ambient can have a wall temperature excess that decays approximately as \(1/x\) away from the source; the natural-convection boundary layer then follows the scaling above. The usual conditions are laminar natural convection, constant properties, vertical orientation, no external crossflow, and \(x\) much larger than the heater size but small enough that boundary-layer and end-effect assumptions remain valid.

The compact statement is that 'the local heat flux varies as "x^{-3/2}," the total rate as x^{-1/2}, and the thickness as x^{1/2}.'
